name: Chloe Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Chloe. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government, and everything you tell me is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do a rural round for an agency called Valley Home Care, so it's about a hundred and twenty miles of lanes a day in my little hatchback. First call is a farmer's widow called Mrs Quayle at seven, then five or six more villages, mostly meals, tablets, washes and checking people haven't fallen. Rural rounds pay a premium plus mileage, so I earn more than town carers. I'm still the new one, to be fair, I've only done eighteen months and I'm clumsy with catheters. The driving in winter is what wears me out, black ice at six in the morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does tech fit into your day, and your life outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI all the time. I talk my visit notes into my phone between villages and let it tidy them up, I use it to plan the route when the roster changes, and I used it to translate for a Polish gentleman until his daughter could visit. At home it's me and my girlfriend Priya, she teaches at the primary school. We've no kids and we're careful, so we've got about nine months of costs saved and a bit in an index fund I set up on an app. I'm in an online network of care workers pushing for better pay and rules on care tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what a shame, honestly, because I like the tools. At work I'd say at least nobody's job changes. Online I'd joke that the robot apocalypse got cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit disappointed, but my job's fine. Rural care is short of people and that won't change. The pay's decent, I've savings, and Priya's job is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the round and keep using the voice notes and route planner, since they still help. I'd keep putting a few hundred into the index fund each month. I might start the moving and handling refresher, because I need to get better at the hands-on bits anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Nothing exciting, nothing scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rural care is short of people. How short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Valley has three rounds with nobody on them right now, so those people get one visit a day instead of three. Out in the villages the real danger isn't robots, it's an old man waiting until noon for his breakfast because nobody applied.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your money in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep saving, maybe buy a house with Priya in a couple of years. Houses round here aren't cheap, but with both our wages we'd manage. I'd want somewhere with a garage for the car in winter.

At work I'd say at least nobody's **job changes**.
think: I'd be a bit **disappointed**, because I like the tools.
Rural care is **short of people**, so my job and pay stay safe.
do: Keep using **voice notes** and the route planner on my round.
Put a few hundred into the **index fund** each month.
Take the **moving and handling** refresher to improve hands-on skills.
S0.quote: Out in the villages the real danger isn't robots, it's an old man waiting until noon for his breakfast because nobody applied.
fieldNote: She is a daily **AI user** in a hands-on job, mostly for notes and routes.
She sees **staff shortages**, not technology, as the real rural danger.
Her savings and partner's teaching wage make her feel **secure**.

steps.text: Keep the Valley rural round with voice notes and route planning
Put a few hundred a month into the index fund
Book the moving and handling refresher course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let the AI take the paperwork and give carers more time with people. But I'd also say we need rules so agencies don't pocket the savings. I'd post about that in the care workers' network.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well. I already use the tools, so I'd be the one showing the others how. My hands-on bit stays because robots are slow to spread, especially down farm tracks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to be Valley's tech champion, helping other carers with the new system, and ask for a bit more pay for it. I'd look at a short course on assistive technology, like fall sensors and smart pill boxes. And I'd keep the savings going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. I'd feel useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work might struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our coordinator, Gwen, books all the rounds by phone and spreadsheet. If an AI books the rounds, my coordinator Gwen loses the part of her job she's proudest of. I'd want her moved into something like family liaison, not let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Priya see it the same way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not quite. Teaching has a lot of marking and planning, so she thinks the thinking AI comes for her before me. We argue about it at dinner sometimes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs public rules right now, and carers need to be in the room when robots go into homes. I'd be organising in the network, maybe a petition. I'd also tell people not to panic, because I'm one who tells people not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, two years for AGI and three more for robots is too fast for me to build a new career. I'm not even good at the job I have yet. I think by 2031 the agencies will run robots on the town rounds first and keep people on the far villages a bit longer, but not forever. And Priya's job gets hit by the thinking AI in 2028, so both of us in the same few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd look for a job with the companies putting robots into homes, as someone who knows both the care and the tech. I'd start a proper course in assistive technology, evenings. I'd keep our savings safe and stop putting new money into the index fund, and we'd hold off on the house. I'd join the petition for rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I won't lie. Excited a bit too, which feels wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it feels wrong to be excited. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people like Mrs Quayle would get a machine instead of me, and I'd be helping set it up. I'd be the one teaching the robot how my client Mrs Quayle likes her tea, and I'd hate myself a bit for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Priya cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house plan, straight away. Then the holiday to the coast. We'd live off one wage if we had to and keep the other saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan properly, so let's do it with carers involved. I'd be pushing in the network for training funded by the agencies. I'd be pretty upbeat in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is a sweet spot for me. I can finish a qualification, get good at the tech, and be ready when the robots come around 2034. The thinking side, like rosters and notes, I'd already be on top of by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an occupational therapy assistant course next year, because it's about helping people adapt their homes, which fits robots too. I'd keep the index fund going and maybe buy the house with Priya, since we'd have a few years of income. I'd keep using AI for everything I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, a bit uneasy about the people who'll lose out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The carers who can't drive long rounds or learn the apps, often older women who've done this forever. And the clients who'll get less human contact. I'd want rules that every person still gets a human visit at least once a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be doing care in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a different kind, setting up the robots and checking on people. I'd rather be the person who decides what the robot does in a stranger's kitchen than the person it replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, let's use it. I'd tell people in the network that we can design how robots and carers work together. I'd sound excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine. By 2039 I'd be thirty-seven with a qualification and years of experience with the tech. The thinking AI comes in 2036, which mostly takes the admin I already let AI do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the occupational therapy assistant course, maybe the full degree later. We'd buy the house in the next two years. I'd keep investing and keep going with the network, maybe stand for something on its committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. It feels like enough time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Quayle and people like her, who'll be gone or very old by then. And whether the agencies share the money they save. Ten years is time for carers like me to adapt, but only if somebody makes the agencies share what the robots save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd have time to move into something like special needs support, which is more hands-on. We've talked about it already. Ten years is enough for both of us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Priya and I could both be hit in the same few years and I'm not good enough at my job yet. What would help is funded training in care technology and rules that make agencies share what they save with carers and clients.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the driving. Nobody thinks about it. A robot might wash someone fine, but a robot driving a farm track in black ice at six in the morning is something I'd pay to see.

headlineQuote: A robot might wash someone fine, but a robot driving a farm track in black ice at six in the morning is something I'd pay to see.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old** rural agency carer, eighteen months in, still clumsy with some hands-on tasks.
She uses **AI daily** for notes, routes and translation, and has nine months saved plus an **index fund**.
She is calm in the slow pictures and expects to **gain** from Steady Disruption.
AGI by 2028 makes her **anxious**, mostly because Priya's teaching job is exposed too.
She would work with **robot firms** but wants rules that protect clients and carers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and **Priya** could both lose income in the same few years.
whatWouldHelp: Rules making agencies **share savings** with carers and clients.
